text: Abraham was now old, well advanced in years, and the LORD had blessed him in every way.
So Abraham said to the senior servant of his household, the one in charge of all he owned, "Place your hand under my thigh,
and I will make you swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and the God of earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I live,
but will go to my own land and to my own kindred and take a wife for my son Isaac."
The servant said to him, "What if the woman is unwilling to come with me to this land? Should I then take your son back to the land you came from?"
"See to it that you do not take my son back there," Abraham said.

"The LORD, the God of heaven, who took me from my father's house and from the land of my birth, who spoke to me and swore to me, 'To your offspring I will give this land' — he will send his angel ahead of you, and you will take a wife for my son from there.
And if the woman is unwilling to come with you, then you are released from this oath of mine. Only do not take my son back there."
So the servant placed his hand under the thigh of his master Abraham and swore to him concerning this matter.
Then the servant took ten of his master's camels and set out, carrying with him all kinds of costly gifts from his master. He made his way to Aram Naharaim, to the city of Nahor.
He had the camels kneel down outside the city by the well of water. It was evening, the time when the women come out to draw water.
And he said, "LORD, God of my master Abraham, grant me success today, and show kindness to my master Abraham.
Here I stand by the spring, and the daughters of the men of the city are coming out to draw water.

Let it be that the young woman to whom I say, 'Please tip your jar so I may drink,' and who answers, 'Drink, and I will water your camels as well' — let her be the one you have chosen for your servant Isaac. By this I will know that you have shown kindness to my master."
Before he had finished speaking, there came Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel son of Milcah, who was the wife of Abraham's brother Nahor. She had her jar on her shoulder.
The young woman was very beautiful, a virgin; no man had ever been with her. She went down to the spring, filled her jar, and came up again.

versions.text: The young woman was very beautiful, a virgin; no man had known her. She went down to the spring, filled her jar, and came up again.
versions.explanation: "Known her" is a Hebraism that can be unclear or even misheard when read aloud. "Had ever been with her" conveys the same sense of יְדָעָהּ plainly and preserves the rhythm of the line.

text: The servant hurried to meet her and said, "Please give me a little water from your jar."
"Drink, my lord," she said, and she quickly lowered the jar to her hand and gave him a drink.
When she had finished giving him a drink, she said, "I will draw water for your camels too, until they have finished drinking."
She quickly emptied her jar into the trough, ran back to the well to draw more, and drew enough for all his camels.
The man watched her in silence, wondering whether the LORD had made his journey a success or not.
When the camels had finished drinking, the man took out a gold nose ring weighing half a shekel and two gold bracelets for her wrists weighing ten shekels.

versions.text: When the camels had finished drinking, the man took out a gold nose ring weighing half a shekel and two gold bracelets weighing ten shekels for her wrists.
versions.explanation: Placing "for her wrists" immediately after "bracelets" (as in the Hebrew word order, שְׁנֵי צְמִידִים עַל־יָדֶיהָ) avoids the awkward hearing that the ten shekels belong to the wrists. A footnote explaining that a beka is about half a shekel (roughly 6 grams) and that the shekel is a weight, not a coin, would also help the listener.

text: He asked, "Whose daughter are you? Please tell me, is there room in your father's house for us to spend the night?"
She answered, "I am the daughter of Bethuel, the son whom Milcah bore to Nahor."
And she added, "We have plenty of straw and fodder, and room for you to spend the night."
Then the man bowed down and worshiped the LORD,

saying, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who has not withheld his kindness and faithfulness from my master. As for me, the LORD has led me on the journey to the house of my master's relatives."
The young woman ran and told her mother's household all that had happened.
Now Rebekah had a brother named Laban, and he ran out to the man at the spring.

versions.text: Now Rebekah had a brother named Laban, and he hurried out to the man at the spring.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb is רוּץ, "ran," the same verb used of the servant (v. 17) and of Rebekah (v. 28). "Ran" keeps the deliberate repetition of running that ties the scene together and is also stronger for oral reading.

text: When he saw the nose ring and the bracelets on his sister's wrists, and heard Rebekah say, "This is what the man said to me," he went out to the man and found him standing with the camels by the spring.

versions.text: As soon as he had seen the nose ring and the bracelets on his sister's wrists and had heard Rebekah tell what the man had said to her, he went out to the man and found him standing with the camels near the spring.
versions.explanation: The current sentence stacks two long "had" clauses before the main verb, which is heavy for reading aloud. Simple past tense with the direct quotation (as in the Hebrew לֵאמֹר כֹּה־דִבֶּר אֵלַי הָאִישׁ) is both closer to the original and easier to follow orally.

text: "Come in, you who are blessed by the LORD," he said. "Why stand out here? I have prepared the house and a place for the camels."
So the man came into the house. The camels were unloaded and given straw and fodder, and water was brought for him and his men to wash their feet.
Then food was set before him, but he said, "I will not eat until I have told you what I have to say." "Speak," said Laban.
So he said, "I am Abraham's servant.
The LORD has blessed my master abundantly, and he has become wealthy. He has given him sheep and cattle, silver and gold, male and female servants, camels and donkeys.
My master's wife Sarah bore him a son in her old age, and he has given him everything he owns.
My master made me swear an oath and said, 'You must not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, in whose land I live,
but go to my father's house and to my own clan, and take a wife for my son.'
Then I said to my master, 'What if the woman will not come with me?'
He answered, 'The LORD, before whom I have walked, will send his angel with you and make your journey a success, so that you may take a wife for my son from my own clan and from my father's house.
Then you will be released from my oath when you come to my clan; and if they will not give her to you, you will be free from my oath.'

versions.text: You will be released from my oath if, when you come to my clan, they refuse to give her to you — then you will be free from my oath.'
versions.explanation: The Hebrew contains two distinct statements: the servant is cleared of the oath once he reaches the clan, and additionally he is free if they refuse. The current wording collapses these into a single condition, making release depend only on a refusal, which changes the sense of the oath.

versions.text: You will be released from my oath when you come to my clan; and if they will not give her to you, you will be free from my oath.'
versions.explanation: The Hebrew opens with אָז ("then"), a discourse connective linking this verse to the condition stated in the previous verse. Rendering it supplies the logical link and gives the sentence a smoother opening cadence for oral reading, without altering the two-part sense established in the earlier revision.

text: "When I came to the spring today, I said, 'LORD, God of my master Abraham, if you will, grant success to the journey I have undertaken.
Here I stand by the spring. Let it be that when a young woman comes out to draw water and I say to her, "Please give me a little water from your jar to drink,"
and she answers, "Drink, and I will draw water for your camels too" — let her be the woman the LORD has chosen for my master's son.'
"Before I had finished praying in my heart, Rebekah came out with her jar on her shoulder. She went down to the spring and drew water, and I said to her, 'Please give me a drink.'
She quickly lowered her jar from her shoulder and said, 'Drink, and I will water your camels too.' So I drank, and she watered the camels as well.
Then I asked her, 'Whose daughter are you?' She said, 'The daughter of Bethuel son of Nahor, whom Milcah bore to him.' So I put the ring in her nose and the bracelets on her wrists,
and I bowed down and worshiped the LORD. I praised the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who had led me on the right road to take the daughter of my master's kinsman for his son.
Now then, if you will show kindness and faithfulness to my master, tell me; and if not, tell me, so that I may turn to the right or to the left."
Laban and Bethuel answered, "This comes from the LORD; we can say nothing to you, one way or the other.
Here is Rebekah; take her and go. Let her become the wife of your master's son, as the LORD has spoken."
When Abraham's servant heard their words, he bowed to the ground before the LORD.
Then the servant brought out objects of silver and gold and fine garments and gave them to Rebekah, and he gave costly gifts to her brother and her mother.

versions.text: Then he brought out silver and gold jewelry and articles of clothing and gave them to Rebekah, and he gave costly gifts to her brother and her mother.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew names the subject ("the servant"), which helps oral clarity after the preceding verse. "Objects of silver and gold" is closer to כלי־כסף וכלי זהב than "jewelry," and "garments" reads more smoothly aloud than "articles of clothing."

text: Then he and the men who were with him ate and drank and spent the night there. When they got up in the morning, he said, "Send me on my way to my master."
But her brother and her mother replied, "Let the girl remain with us a while, ten days or so; after that she may go."
But he said to them, "Do not detain me, now that the LORD has made my journey a success. Send me on my way so I may go to my master."
They said, "Let us call the girl and ask her."
So they called Rebekah and asked her, "Will you go with this man?" "I will go," she said.
So they sent their sister Rebekah on her way, along with her nurse, together with Abraham's servant and his men.
And they blessed Rebekah, saying to her, "Our sister, may you become the mother of thousands upon thousands; may your offspring possess the gates of their enemies."
Then Rebekah and her maids mounted the camels and followed the man. So the servant took Rebekah and set out.
Now Isaac had come from the direction of Beer Lahai Roi, for he was living in the region of the Negev.
One evening he went out to the field to meditate, and as he looked up, he saw camels approaching.
Rebekah also looked up and saw Isaac, and she got down from her camel.
She asked the servant, "Who is that man coming through the field to meet us?" "He is my master," the servant answered. So she took her veil and covered herself.
Then the servant told Isaac everything he had done.
Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother Sarah, and he took Rebekah as his wife. He loved her, and Isaac was comforted after his mother's death.
